opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a useful contrast, and I don't mean it as a moral judgment on the people at either company, but the business models are really quite different, and that shapes what kind of technology gets built.

Amazon, at its core, is a market. It connects producers and consumers. There's a seller who has something, a buyer who wants something, and Amazon sits in the middle and makes that transaction happen more efficiently. The machine learning there, the recommendation systems, the supply chain optimization, the logistics, all of that is in service of creating a two-sided relationship where value actually flows. Somebody gets a book, somebody gets paid for the book. Money changes hands, and that's a signal. It tells you something about what people actually value, and it creates an incentive for the producers to keep producing good things.

Meta's model is fundamentally advertising. The users aren't really the customers in the economic sense; the advertisers are. And so the technology gets optimized for attention, for engagement, for keeping you on the platform so that you can be shown ads. The content creators, the people actually producing the stuff that people come for, are mostly not in an economic relationship with the consumers at all. There's no market there linking them. The value gets extracted by the platform in the middle.

And I think that matters a lot for how we think about AI going forward. The narrative right now is very much about building these big, intelligent systems, this sort of superintelligence in a box, and then the business model is an afterthought, often ending up as advertising or something like it. Whereas I'd argue the more interesting, and frankly more beneficial, thing is to think about machine learning as a way to create new markets, new connections between people. Think about music: you could have a platform where a young musician is linked directly to listeners who love their stuff, and data flows and money flows and the musician can actually make a living. That's an economic and social system, not just a prediction engine.

So for me the distinction is between technology that creates value by building markets and connecting people, where there's a signal of genuine value, versus technology that captures value by harvesting attention. Amazon's not perfect by any means, but it's closer to the first. And I think as a field, machine learning people need to think much more like economists about this, about incentives, about who benefits, and not just about the accuracy of the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the distinction is really about where the value gets created and who it flows to. Amazon, whatever else you want to say about it, built a marketplace. There's a two-sided structure there: producers and consumers, buyers and sellers, and the technology is in service of making those matches happen more efficiently. Recommendation systems, logistics, the whole machinery of it. And the key thing is that when a transaction happens, value gets created for both sides. A small seller somewhere can reach customers they never would have reached, and the customer gets something they actually wanted. Money changes hands, there's a real economic exchange, and the data is being used to make that exchange better. I'm not saying it's perfect, there are monopoly concerns and all of that, but the underlying economic model is one where the participants are actually participating.

Meta is a different story. The user is not the customer. The user is the product, or more precisely the user's attention is the product, and the actual customers are the advertisers. So all of the machine learning, all of the prediction and ranking and recommendation, is aimed at keeping you engaged so that your attention can be sold. There's no market that includes you. You don't get paid when your data turns out to be valuable, you don't have any mechanism for expressing what you actually want out of the system, and the incentives are fundamentally misaligned with your interests. It's a very old business model dressed up in very new technology.

And this is the thing I keep coming back to. The machine learning community has been obsessed with the individual agent, the single intelligence, the prediction problem. But the interesting problems are collective. They're about markets, about incentives, about how you design systems where lots of people with different goals and different information can interact and all come out ahead. Economics has thought about this for a couple of hundred years. Amazon stumbled into something that at least resembles a market. Meta built something that resembles a casino. If we want this technology to actually create value, broadly, we need to be designing the market structures on purpose, not treating them as an afterthought to the algorithm.

astra-6.text:
I’d draw the distinction in terms of the economic relationships they organize. Amazon helps people find and buy things, but it also provides infrastructure that other businesses can use to sell things and build services. There’s a fairly direct connection between the technology and an economic transaction: someone has something to offer, someone else wants it, and the system helps bring them together.

Meta’s core business is organized around attention and advertising. People get value from communicating with one another, but the paying customer is typically an advertiser. So there’s a separation between the person using the service and the person paying for it, and that shapes the incentives.

Both use machine learning extensively. The interesting distinction isn’t whose prediction algorithm is better; it’s what system those predictions serve. Are you helping participants find mutually beneficial transactions? How is value distributed? And does improving the system’s objective actually improve the outcome for the people involved?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is clearest if you look at the economic relationships they enable. Amazon helps people find things, but it also provides infrastructure through which other people can build businesses. With AWS, for example, the value is that someone else can create a service without first building a data center. There’s a fairly direct connection between the technology and an economic activity somebody wants to undertake.

Meta’s central business is organized around attention and advertising. People connect and share things, and the platform uses the resulting information to decide what to show them, including ads. That creates value too, but the incentives are different: the person using the service and the person paying for it are different parties.

Now, Amazon has an advertising business, and neither company fits neatly into a single category. But the distinction I care about is between building infrastructure that enables productive interactions and optimizing engagement within a platform. For machine learning, that raises a much richer question than prediction accuracy: what kind of system are we building, who benefits from it, and how do we align the incentives of everyone participating?
